claims.text: The onset of yielding in single-crystal FeNiCrMn is dominated by thermally activated dislocation nucleation and glide rather than phase transformation.
FeNiCrMn has anomalously low yield-strength sensitivity to strain rate compared with traditional FCC metals.
The FCC matrix contains substantial lattice distortion and chemical short-range order.
Lattice distortion and CSRO create a high density of local energy barriers to dislocation nucleation and glide.
Thermal fluctuations overcome the local barriers and thereby reduce the strain-rate dependence of yield stress.
Yielding involves nucleation of partial dislocations at surface defects or pre-existing dislocation sources.
Twinning-induced plasticity is operative at cryogenic temperature.
Dislocation and stacking-fault accumulation causes martensitic transformation to an HCP phase at low temperature.
At temperatures up to 600 K, thermal activation unlocks dislocations from Lomer-Cottrell locks and maintains ductility.
The <001> tensile orientation has the highest yield strength because of FCC slip-system geometry.
The <111> and <101> orientations have lower yield strengths and greater deformation anisotropy than <001>.
The initial single-crystal FeNiCrMn alloy has an FCC structure.
The initial alloy is compositionally homogeneous.
The initial alloy has a low dislocation density.
At high temperature, dislocation slip and HCP-phase accumulation dominate deformation.
No BCC phase transformation occurs during yielding or subsequent plastic deformation.
Pure Ni and Cu have higher yield-strength strain-rate sensitivity because they have lower lattice distortion and no CSRO.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply above 600 K because phase instability may occur.

Absence of BCC diffraction peaks and BCC lattice signatures during in-situ loading at 600 K would falsify the proposition that FCC-to-BCC transformation is the primary deformation mode at that boundary condition.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis initially states that yielding is dominated by dislocation processes rather than phase transformation, but the mechanism and predicted outcome assign an important or dominant role to martensitic HCP phase transformation without clearly limiting the initial statement to FCC-to-BCC transformation.

The mechanism associates HCP martensitic transformation with low temperatures and high-temperature behavior with dislocation unlocking, whereas the predicted outcome additionally states that HCP-phase accumulation dominates at high temperature.
